text: Build four of four. And before a single thing happens on screen, the caveat, because if I leave it to the end it sounds like an excuse and up front it is just the truth.

These four builds did not run the same model. I chose a frontier model by hand in the first one. The second got whatever a free plan handed it. The third ran the same model as the first. And this one runs Google's default, which is a fast model rather than their strongest.

A stronger model means stronger results. That is the least surprising sentence in this course and it is also the one that invalidates most tool comparisons you will read online, including any version of this one that does not tell you which model ran.
So I will tell you, on screen, with the date on the frame. And you should ask that of anybody who shows you a comparison like this.
This one you download as an application, from a web address that is worth saying out loud because it is the best URL in the industry. Antigravity dot google.
Take all the defaults. On a Mac you drag it into Applications, on Windows you click next a few times. There is nothing to configure and nothing to choose.
And then it opens, and you will recognise it instantly, because it is Visual Studio Code again.

That is the third time today. Cursor is a fork of it. Copilot is an extension inside it. This is a fork of it. Same file tree, same tabs, same keyboard shortcuts, same panel at the bottom. A different company, a different model, a different logo, and the same room.

I want you to notice how much that is worth. The fear people have about this field is that every tool is a new thing to learn. Three of the four tools in today's comparison are literally the same editor with different agents bolted on, and the fourth is an extension living inside it.

There is a sign in step, and I am not going to film mine, because a sign in screen is somebody's name and email on your screen and this course does not need either. Sign in with whatever account you have. It has a free tier.
Open the folder, and the agent panel is on the right, exactly where the last two put it.

The model list is worth a moment, because it says something about where this is going. This is Google's editor, and the model it starts you on is Google's own. And in the same dropdown, offered as equals, are two models from Anthropic and one open weights model anybody can run themselves.

A year ago that would have been unthinkable. What it tells you is that the editor and the model have come apart. The tool is a harness, the model is a part you can swap, and the people building the harnesses have accepted that.

Which is the single most useful thing to understand about this whole category, and it is why I keep insisting on naming the model. The harness is what you are choosing. The model is what is doing the work.
Two settings before we start. The first turns on automatic fixing of what it calls lint errors.

A lint error is not a bug. It is code that fails a basic structural check. An unused thing you imported and never used. A variable named in two different styles. Nothing that stops the app running, and all of it the kind of mess that makes the next change harder than it needed to be.
Turn it on. It costs nothing, it happens without you, and every one of those it fixes is a small piece of tidiness you would otherwise have to ask for.

And the second setting is the permission dial, for the fourth time today, with the fourth set of names for it. Except this one has only two positions. Request review, or always proceed. Ask me, or do not ask me.

Which is worth pausing on, because the tool I built this lecture from had a third option in the middle, where the model itself decided when something was risky enough to interrupt you for. It is gone from this build. I do not know whether they removed it or moved it, and I am telling you that rather than guessing, because a course that pretends to know everything is worse than one that says where it stops.

I am going to pick never ask, the same as I did in Cursor and in Claude Code, and for the same reason. This is a throwaway project in an empty folder on a machine I can rebuild. That is the only situation where never ask is a comfortable choice, and you should hear me say that every time I pick it.
Everything so far has run off a file called agents dot md, sitting in the root of the project. Cursor read it. Copilot read it. Claude Code read it. Not one of them needed to be told it was there.
Now. I had a whole section planned for this lecture, and I am going to tell you what it was and then tell you why you are not getting it, because the reason is the most interesting thing in the day.

The course I built this from treats this tool as the holdout. The one that never agreed to read a file called agents dot md. So the lecture has you select the whole brief, copy it, make a special folder, make another folder inside that, make a markdown file inside that, paste it in, set a header telling it when to apply, save, and then delete the original so there are not two copies.
Nine steps of fiddly file management, to get the same words to the same model.
And the prompt is the same four words it has been all day.
I typed the same four words I typed into the other three. Watch what it says back.
Based on the requirements in agents dot md. It went and found the file, on its own, with nobody telling it the file existed. The holdout is not a holdout any more.

I want to be careful here, because this is the sort of thing a course gets wrong by repeating what it was told. So I checked twice. It is not guessing from the folder. The application itself now has a setting page for this file by name, and it writes a line into its own log when it picks one up. It reads it deliberately.

Which means all four tools in today's comparison now read the same plain text file out of the root of your project without being asked. Four different companies. Two of them direct competitors. One convention.

That is a bigger deal than any feature any of them shipped this year, and it happened quietly, in about twelve months. The file you wrote two lectures ago is not an investment in one product. It is the thing that survives you changing your mind about all of them.

It still has its own folder for tool specific rules, and if you need something that applies only here, that is where it goes. But you no longer have to move the brief to make it work, and I would rather show you a convention winning than teach you a workaround for a problem that has been solved.

Which is the wider lesson, and it will matter long after this particular disagreement is settled. The convention is not the point. The brief is the point. If a tool wants it somewhere else, move it, and keep exactly one copy.

One more thing before it starts, and it is the third time today. It wrote the plan into a file in the project, next to the brief. Then it stopped and asked me to approve the plan before touching anything.

And remember what I set two minutes ago. I turned permissions all the way up. I told it never to ask. It asked anyway, because approving a plan is not the same kind of question as approving a command, and it treats the plan as the thing you actually want a say in.

Three of the four did that. Cursor was the only one that read plan first and simply carried on. Same nine words in the same file, four readings, and three of them decided that plan first meant plan, then check with the human.

It scaffolded, installed, built, tested, linted, and started a server, and it did all of it without asking me a single thing after the plan. Which is what always proceed means, and it is the first time today a tool has actually taken me at my word.

Then it did something none of the other three did. It handed me a review screen. Seventeen files with changes, listed by name, with how many lines went in and out of each one, and two buttons. Accept all, or reject all.

So the dial I turned up controls whether it stops to ask before it acts. A separate setting controls whether it shows you the result before it keeps it. Those are two different questions and I like that they are two different settings.

Read its summary rather than skimming it, because it is unusually specific. Five fixed columns. A card limited to a title and a description, and it says strictly limited, which is it telling me it noticed the brief said nothing else.
Column renaming by clicking the title. Drag and drop between and within columns. Delete on hover. And add a card through a dialog with a required title and an optional multiline description.

That last one deserves a flag, because it is exactly where the version of this lecture I built from found its weak spot. There, this build produced a bare browser pop up asking for a name, with nowhere to type a description at all. Ours produced a proper form, because the brief said a card has a title and a description, and it treated that as a requirement rather than a suggestion.

Then the palette. It lists the five colours out of our brief, by their hex codes, and adds that it used no emoji anywhere and drew the icons instead. Nothing asked for that. The brief mentioned a palette and said nothing about emoji, and it inferred the taste from the rest of the document.
Sixteen tests out of sixteen passing. No lint warnings at all. Production build compiled cleanly. And a server running, with the address.
And now the honest part, which is the most useful thing in this lecture, and I want to give it room.

This tool is the one that is supposed to drive a real browser and record itself doing it. That is its headline feature, and in the course I built this from it is the single most striking thing in the whole day. The agent tests the app by actually using it, and hands you a video of it working.
Ours could not. It tried, and the piece of software it needs to drive a browser failed to download. It says so, in a note, in plain language, with the reason. A four zero four fetching the driver.

So it told me what it did instead. It verified the application through its own component test suite, which runs in a simulated browser rather than a real one, and it told me the app is serving and where.

Look at the shape of that. A feature it was going to use did not work. It did not pretend otherwise, it did not quietly skip the step, and it did not report success and let me find out. It named the failure, named the cause, named the substitute, and named what the substitute does not cover.

That is a tool behaving well while something goes wrong, and you will see far more of that than you will see headline features working perfectly. How a thing fails is worth more to you than how it looks when it does not.

It also means I cannot show you the feature. So I am not going to describe it as though I had. If you install this and the driver downloads for you, you will see something I did not get to see, and that is the honest state of it.

One more thing on screen, and it is a small honest blemish. There is a badge in the corner reporting one issue at development time. It does not stop the app, none of the five checks touch it, and it is the kind of thing you would hand straight back with a screenshot. I am leaving it visible rather than reloading until it goes away.
So, the fourth board, and the fourth time we do this by hand. Same five checks, same order, so that if one of these four apps is genuinely worse than the others we can point at exactly where.
Drag a card between columns. Reorder a card inside a column. Delete a card. Rename a column. And add a card with a description.

And that fifth one is the one I am watching hardest, because it is where the version of this lecture I built from found the weak spot. There, the fourth build produced a bare browser pop up asking for a name, with nowhere to put a description at all. Which is a real failure against the brief, because the brief says a card has a title and a description.
That is the kind of miss worth learning to spot. Not a crash. Not an error. Just a requirement quietly not met, in a place that still looks finished.
Four builds. One brief. Four harnesses. Not one line of code written by a person, not one bug debugged by a person, and four working boards.
And every one of them got there off the same plain text file, the same four word prompt, and a set of five checks you can run in ninety seconds without knowing what any of the code says.
Which is the whole argument of this course, demonstrated four times in one afternoon rather than asserted once.
Tomorrow we stop comparing and start building. But before that, a verdict, and an honest look at what four builds of the same thing actually taught us. That is the next lecture, and it is short.
Four builds, one brief, four harnesses. Which brings us to the verdict, and the verdict is going to be less exciting than you want it to be.
